tagline.text: A miracle of a marine sanctuary where you swim beside sea turtles

image.credit: Mike Gonzalez (TheCoffee) / CC BY-SA 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.credit: Anna Varona / CC BY 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A small volcanic island in the sea south of Dumaguete, where a marine protected area the residents have guarded themselves makes it almost certain you'll meet sea turtles in the shallows. It is a model case of Filipino community-based marine conservation and a world-class diving destination.
Apo Island is a small volcanic island of about 0.7 km² lying roughly
7km

off the southeastern coast of Negros. Administratively part of Dauin, it is home to around 1,000 residents who live by fishing and tourism. It shares its name with Mount Apo in Mindanao but is an entirely different place, so don't confuse the two. The island's west side has the village and a sand beach, its east side has rocky cliffs, and coral reef surrounds the whole island.
What made this island world famous lies less in the sea itself than in "how it was protected." When dynamite fishing and overfishing collapsed the coral reefs in the
, Silliman University marine biologist Dr. Angel Alcala worked with residents to designate part of the island's southeast as a no-fishing zone around

. As residents patrolled and enforced the rules themselves, fish returned within a few years, and catches even increased outside the no-fishing zone. It was later designated a protected landscape and seascape in
, becoming a world-renowned model of community-based marine protection.
Today, more than 650 fish species and over 400 coral species have been recorded in Apo Island's waters. The island's biggest draw for travelers is that at depths of just
, you can see green and hawksbill sea turtles grazing on seagrass almost every time. Even if you're not a strong swimmer, wearing a life vest and following a guide lets you enjoy it fully.

For divers, the east wall with its strong currents and coral gardens await. The island satisfies a wide range of visitors, from families wanting turtle snorkeling to experienced divers hoping to see schools of jackfish, to travelers who just want a quiet night on an island with limited electricity.
In the shallow waters in front of the village, you can get a close look at sea turtles grazing on seagrass. A guide is mandatory, and you must keep a distance of at least
4m
from the turtles without touching or chasing them.

blocks.title: Diving in the protected coral garden

children.text: Around the protected area on the island's southeast, table coral and soft coral grow densely, and if you're lucky you'll encounter schools of jackfish and barracuda. Diving within the protected area is managed by headcount and frequency, so book through a local dive shop.

Coconut Point on the island's northeast is known for drift diving carried by the current, while Chapel Point to the west is relatively gentle and popular with intermediate divers. Currents are often strong, so always follow your guide's judgment.
From the village, following steps and a dirt path for about
20–30 minutes
brings you to the lighthouse near the island's summit. On a clear day you can see the main island of Negros, Siquijor, and even as far as Mindanao.

blocks.title: Village walk and hearing the conservation story

children.text: The small village has a marine sanctuary management office, a school, and souvenir stalls. Buying t-shirts and handkerchiefs made by residents sends the proceeds back to the community.

blocks.title: Spending a night on the island

children.text: From the afternoon when the day-trippers leave, the island becomes surprisingly quiet. You can watch the sun set into the western sea and see the stars in a night sky with almost no electric light.

blocks.title: Stopping by the Malatapay Wednesday market

children.text: At Malatapay, where the boats to the island depart, a livestock market and lechon (whole roast pig) stalls open every Wednesday. It's a good place to look around before catching an early boat.

It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila to Dumaguete (Sibulan Airport, DGT). Coming from Cebu, boats and buses are more convenient than flying.
Boats to Apo Island depart from Malatapay port in Zamboanguita, about
25km
south of Dumaguete. Taking a bus or jeepney bound for Bais or Siaton from Dumaguete's southern bus terminal or roadside and getting off at the Malatapay turnoff takes about
40–60 minutes
, for a fare of about
. Chartering a tricycle costs about
one way. From a Dauin beach resort, it's about
15–20 minutes
away.
From Malatapay to Apo Island takes about
30–45 minutes
by bangka. There is no scheduled passenger ferry; instead you charter a boat through the bangka association at the port. A round-trip charter on a small bangka costs about

(for 4–6 people), and if you're alone, joining other travelers at the port is more economical. The easiest option is a day tour from a Dumaguete or Dauin dive shop, which includes pickup, bangka, snorkel gear, lunch, and a guide for about
per person.
From Cebu's South Bus Terminal, a bus to Liloan port near Oslob takes about
3–4 hours
, then a boat to Sibulan port takes about
30 minutes
, and another car ride south to Malatapay takes about
1 hour
. Reaching the island in a single day is tight, so it's better to stay overnight in Dumaguete or Dauin and depart the next morning.
How enjoyable the trip to Apo Island is depends heavily on the waves. From
March
to
June
, the sea is calmest and the water warmest, with visibility often reaching
. From
December
to
February
, the northeast monsoon (Amihan) blows and afternoon waves can pick up on some days, but travel is generally still possible.
Between
July
and
October

, the southwest monsoon (Habagat) and typhoons increase the number of days when bangka trips are canceled. Waves tend to rise especially in the afternoon, so regardless of season, the rule is to depart early in the morning and return by early afternoon. Water temperature stays around 26–29°C year-round, so a thin wetsuit or rash guard is enough.

Most travelers stay in downtown Dumaguete or a Dauin beach resort and visit as a day trip. Dauin has a cluster of resorts running diving packages, making it convenient to head out to the island in the morning. On the island itself there are a few small guesthouses, including the long-running Liberty's Lodge and Apo Island Beach Resort, often around
per night with meals frequently included. Rooms are limited, so book several weeks ahead for peak season.

The island's electricity relies on generators and solar power, supplied for only a few hours in the evening in many places, and rooms without air conditioning are the norm. Meals are taken at the accommodation's kitchen or a small village eatery, mostly simple Filipino home cooking like grilled fish, sautéed vegetables, and rice. The lechon and grilled fish sold at the mainland's Malatapay Wednesday market are a local specialty, so be sure to try them if your schedule allows.
The island has no ATMs and card payments are rarely accepted, so bring enough cash for the environmental fee, guide fee, and meals.
Cell signal only reaches parts of the island, so confirm arrangements with your accommodation and boatman in advance.
To protect the coral reef, use reef-safe sunscreen or cover your skin with a rash guard and leggings.
The turtle zone in front of the village is calmest around
, and gets crowded after
10 AM
when day-tour boats arrive.
If you're not a confident swimmer, wear a life vest and stay close to your guide; fins help a lot in cutting fatigue from the current.
When filming turtles with a waterproof camera or action cam, turn off the flash and shoot from above so as not to disturb them.
If you're prone to seasickness, take medication
30 minutes
before boarding the bangka and sit toward the back.
Island guests should bring a flashlight (headlamp), a portable battery, and mosquito repellent.
Touching, chasing, or riding turtles, and stepping on coral, are strictly prohibited and can result in fines and expulsion if caught.
The currents on the island's east and south points are very strong and can sweep snorkelers away, so only enter the water in areas your guide permits.
Waves tend to rise in the afternoon, so if the boatman suggests moving up the return time, it's safer to follow.
Entry rules, the environmental fee, and daily visitor limits can change based on decisions by the protected area management committee, so check the latest notices before departing.
The island has no hospital, so disinfect wounds immediately, and be sure to treat coral cuts once back on the main island, since they're prone to infection.
Jellyfish and sea urchin stings occur, so don't walk barefoot on shallow rocky areas — wear aqua shoes.
